claim: Class IV sensory neurons in Drosophila larvae respond to noxious thermal stimuli and provoke heat avoidance behavior.
source: In Drosophila larvae, Class IV sensory neurons respond to noxious thermal stimuli and provoke heat avoidance behavior.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about Class IV neurons.

claim: Activated Class IV neurons display characteristic fluctuations of firing rates consisting of repetitive high-frequency spike trains and subsequent pause periods.
source: Previously, we showed that the activated neurons displayed characteristic fluctuations of firing rates, which consisted of repetitive high-frequency spike trains and subsequent pause periods, and we proposed that the firing rate fluctuations enhanced the heat avoidance (Terada et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Terada et al., 2016).

claim: Firing rate fluctuations in Class IV neurons enhance heat avoidance behavior.
source: Previously, we showed that the activated neurons displayed characteristic fluctuations of firing rates, which consisted of repetitive high-frequency spike trains and subsequent pause periods, and we proposed that the firing rate fluctuations enhanced the heat avoidance (Terada et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed in previous work cited in the manuscript.

claim: The pause periods and the frequency of fluctuations in Class IV neurons are regulated by small conductance Ca2+-activated K+ (SK) channels.
source: Here, we further substantiate this idea by showing that the pause periods and the frequency of fluctuations are regulated by small conductance Ca2+-activated K+ (SK) channels, and the SK knockdown larvae display faster heat avoidance than control larvae.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SK knockdown larvae display faster heat avoidance than control larvae.
source: Here, we further substantiate this idea by showing that the pause periods and the frequency of fluctuations are regulated by small conductance Ca2+-activated K+ (SK) channels, and the SK knockdown larvae display faster heat avoidance than control larvae.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: The regulatory mechanism of fluctuations in Class IV neurons resembles that in mammalian Purkinje cells which display complex spikes.
source: The regulatory mechanism of the fluctuations in the Class IV neurons resembles that in mammalian Purkinje cells, which display complex spikes.
evidence: This is a comparative claim made in the abstract and elaborated in the Discussion section.

claim: Fluctuation coding in Class IV neurons is required to convert noxious thermal inputs into effective stereotyped behavior as well as general rate coding.
source: Furthermore, our results suggest that such fluctuation coding in Class IV neurons is required to convert noxious thermal inputs into effective stereotyped behavior as well as general rate coding.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented in the study.

claim: Sensory neurons convert the intensity of stimuli into the magnitude of firing rates upon sensory transduction.
source: In principle, sensory neurons convert the intensity of stimuli into the magnitude of firing rates upon sensory transduction (Adrian, 1926).
evidence: This is a general principle of sensory neuroscience supported by a historical citation.

claim: Mammalian C-fiber nociceptors convert gentle touch stimuli into relatively low firing rates, whereas injurious forces elicit higher rates.
source: For instance, mammalian C-fiber nociceptors convert gentle touch stimuli into relatively low firing rates, whereas injurious forces elicit higher rates (Delmas et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an example of rate coding in mammalian nociceptors, supported by citation.

claim: Firing rates have an intrinsic upper limit because interspike intervals cannot be shorter than refractory periods.
source: The 'rate coding' is valuable for sensory transduction, particularly with regard to stimulus intensity; however, the firing rate has an intrinsic upper limit because interspike intervals (ISIs) cannot be shorter than refractory periods, when the membrane is unable to respond to another stimulus (Berry and Meister, 1998; Hodgkin and Huxley, 1952).
evidence: This is a fundamental principle of neuronal physiology supported by citations.

claim: Firing rates should saturate at high stimulus intensities, at which point sensory inputs are no longer converted properly in an intensity-to-firing rate correspondence.
source: This implies that firing rates should saturate at high intensities, at which point the sensory inputs are no longer converted properly in an intensity-to-firing rate correspondence.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the principle of refractory periods limiting firing rates.

claim: Some sensory neurons may use coding mechanisms other than rate coding that are employed in the central nervous system.
source: Therefore, we assume that some sensory neurons may use other coding mechanisms that are employed in the central nervous system (Avissar et al., 2013; Haddad et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference and supported by citations to studies of central nervous system coding.

claim: Class IV dendritic arborization neurons are primary nociceptive neurons in Drosophila larvae.
source: In Drosophila larvae, Class IV dendritic arborization neurons (Class IV neurons) are primary nociceptive neurons that respond to multiple stimuli, including high temperature, strong mechanical force, and short-wavelength light (Hwang et al., 2007; Tracey et al., 2003; Xiang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an established fact about Class IV neurons supported by multiple citations.

claim: Class IV neurons respond to multiple stimuli including high temperature, strong mechanical force, and short-wavelength light.
source: In Drosophila larvae, Class IV dendritic arborization neurons (Class IV neurons) are primary nociceptive neurons that respond to multiple stimuli, including high temperature, strong mechanical force, and short-wavelength light (Hwang et al., 2007; Tracey et al., 2003; Xiang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies characterizing Class IV neurons.

claim: When Class IV neurons are activated by noxious thermal stimuli, their sensory transduction provokes heat avoidance behavior where larvae rotate around the long body axis in a corkscrew-like manner.
source: When the neurons are activated by noxious thermal stimuli, for instance, their sensory transduction provokes heat avoidance behavior where larvae rotate around the long body axis in a corkscrew-like manner.
evidence: This describes the behavioral output of Class IV neuron activation, which is established knowledge.

claim: A large number of genes responsible for Class IV neuronal activation were identified by evaluating behavioral phenotypes and monitoring Ca2+ dynamics in mutant strains.
source: A large number of genes responsible for the neuronal activation were identified by evaluating behavioral phenotypes and monitoring Ca2+ dynamics in mutant strains (Lee et al., 2005; Neely et al., 2011; Tracey et al., 2003; Zhong et al., 2012)
evidence: This summarizes previous genetic studies on Class IV neurons, supported by citations.

claim: There have been few studies which have investigated the coding mechanism of nociception in Class IV neurons by recording electrical activity.
source: however, there have been few studies which have investigated the coding mechanism of the nociception by recording electrical activity (Terada et al., 2016; Xiang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field supported by limited citations.

claim: Class IV neurons responded to noxious thermal stimuli with evoked characteristic fluctuations of firing rates consisting of repetitive high-frequency spike trains and subsequent quiescent periods.
source: Previously, we built a measurement system using a 1460 nm infrared (IR) laser as a local heating device (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and found that Class IV neurons responded to noxious thermal stimuli with evoked characteristic fluctuations of firing rates, which consisted of repetitive high-frequency spike trains and subsequent quiescent periods (Terada et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from previous work by the authors, supported by citation and reference to a figure.

claim: The occurrence of burst-and-pause firing patterns was coordinated with large Ca2+ increments over the entire dendritic arbors.
source: The occurrence of such 'burst-and-pause' firing patterns was coordinated with large Ca2+ increments over the entire dendritic arbors (designated as dendritic Ca2+ transients here) and was mediated by L-type voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (VGCCs).
evidence: This is a finding from previous work describing the relationship between firing patterns and Ca2+ dynamics.

claim: Burst-and-pause firing patterns in Class IV neurons are mediated by L-type voltage-gated Ca2+ channels.
source: The occurrence of such 'burst-and-pause' firing patterns was coordinated with large Ca2+ increments over the entire dendritic arbors (designated as dendritic Ca2+ transients here) and was mediated by L-type voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (VGCCs).
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding from previous work.

claim: Knocking down L-type VGCCs in Class IV neurons abolished the burst-and-pause firing patterns.
source: Knocking down L-type VGCCs in neurons abolished the burst-and-pause firing patterns, and the knockdown larvae displayed delayed heat avoidance behavior.
evidence: This is an experimental result from previous work showing the necessity of L-type VGCCs.

claim: L-type VGCC knockdown larvae displayed delayed heat avoidance behavior.
source: Knocking down L-type VGCCs in neurons abolished the burst-and-pause firing patterns, and the knockdown larvae displayed delayed heat avoidance behavior.
evidence: This is a behavioral phenotype observed in previous work.

claim: The burst-and-pause firing patterns should be output signals transducing high intensity stimuli and provoking robust avoidance behavior.
source: Therefore, we hypothesized that the burst-and-pause firing patterns should be output signals transducing high intensity stimuli and provoking the robust avoidance behavior.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on previous findings.

claim: The regulatory mechanism of burst-and-pause firing patterns remained unclear because L-type VGCCs produce depolarizing currents but not hyperpolarizing ones which should underlie pause periods.
source: However, the regulatory mechanism of the firing patterns remained unclear because L-type VGCCs produce depolarizing currents but not hyperpolarizing ones, which should underlie 'pause' periods.
evidence: This identifies a gap in understanding based on the known properties of L-type VGCCs.

claim: All dendritic Ca2+ transients occurred concurrently with unconventional spikes (USs).
source: We then found that all the dendritic Ca2+ transients occurred concurrently with USs (Figure 1B,C and D).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: When no US occurred or before the first US occurred, Ca2+ transients were never observed.
source: In contrast, when no US occurred or before the first US occurred, Ca2+ transients were never observed.
evidence: This is an observation from the current study establishing the relationship between USs and Ca2+ transients.

claim: The onset of Ca2+ transients preceded first-US timings by 50.3 ± 9.2 ms.
source: We then found that the onset of Ca2+ transients preceded first-US timings and that the Ca2+ transients with multiple USs were stepwise (Figure 1E and F; Δt = − 50.3 ± 9.2 ms, mean ± s.e.m.).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the current study using curve fitting analysis.

claim: Ca2+ transients with multiple USs were stepwise.
source: We then found that the onset of Ca2+ transients preceded first-US timings and that the Ca2+ transients with multiple USs were stepwise (Figure 1E and F; Δt = − 50.3 ± 9.2 ms, mean ± s.e.m.).
evidence: This is an observation from the current study describing the temporal structure of Ca2+ transients.

claim: The peak amplitudes of Ca2+ transients displayed a positive linear correlation with the number of USs.
source: We also found that the peak amplitudes of Ca2+ transients displayed a positive linear correlation with the number of USs (Figure 1G; p=1.0 × 10−11, rho = 0.82, Spearman's rank correlation test).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the current study showing a correlation between Ca2+ amplitude and US number.

claim: Interspike intervals (ISIs) were shorter before onsets of pauses.
source: Furthermore, ISIs were shorter before onsets of pauses (Figure 1H; p<0.05, paired-sample t-test with Bonferroni correction).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the current study about the temporal structure of firing patterns.

claim: The Ca2+ influx mediated by L-type VGCCs amplifies membrane depolarization, which narrows down ISIs of bursts and also induces subsequent pauses.
source: We hypothesized that the Ca2+ influx mediated by L-type VGCCs amplifies membrane depolarization, which narrows down ISIs of bursts and also induces subsequent pauses.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the observed firing patterns.

claim: The FRET ratio of SuperClomeleon increased at both somata and distal dendrites upon IR-laser irradiation.
source: We therefore monitored Cl− dynamics by a genetically encoded FRET-based Cl− indicator, SuperClomeleon (Grimley et al., 2013; Figure 2A) and found that the FRET ratio increased at both somata and distal dendrites upon IR-laser irradiation (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the current study using a Cl− indicator.

claim: The intracellular Cl− concentration decreases in Class IV neurons upon stimulation.
source: Because the FRET ratio of SuperClomeleon rises as the [Cl−]i falls, we expected that the [Cl−]i should decrease upon stimulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of the SuperClomeleon indicator and the observed FRET ratio changes.

claim: Passive Cl− transport in Class IV neurons is outward and generates depolarizing currents but not hyperpolarizing ones.
source: These results suggest that the passive Cl− transport in Class IV neurons is outward and generates depolarizing currents but not hyperpolarizing ones.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Cl− imaging data.

claim: Subdued, a Ca2+-activated Cl− channel, can contribute to membrane excitation in Class IV neurons.
source: In parallel, we investigated the role of one of the Ca2+-activated Cl− channels, Subdued (Jang et al., 2015), and showed that it can contribute to membrane excitation in the neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study about the role of Subdued channels.

claim: The number of USs was significantly increased in five different gene knockdown neurons (Sh, Shal, SK, Irk2, and Task7).
source: We found that the number of USs was significantly increased in five different gene knockdown neurons (Sh, Shal, SK, Irk2, and Task7; Figure 2D and E; p<0.05, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiological screen conducted in the current study.

claim: The five K+ channel knockdown neurons (Sh, Shal, SK, Irk2, Task7) exhibited an increased number of peaks in firing rate fluctuations.
source: The five knockdown neurons also exhibited an increased number of 'peaks' (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; p<0.05, Wilcoxon rank sum test), as defined in our previous study (Terada et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study using a different metric for firing rate fluctuations.

claim: The five K+ channel knockdowns (Sh, Shal, SK, Irk2, Task7) did not decrease the amplitudes of dendritic Ca2+ transients.
source: Furthermore, although knocking down L-type VGCC abolishes dendritic Ca2+ transients (Terada et al., 2016), the five K+ channel knockdowns did not decrease the amplitudes of the Ca2+ transients (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study showing that these K+ channels act downstream of Ca2+ influx.

claim: SK channels can be activated by dendritic Ca2+ influx and could be one of the major factors underlying hyperpolarization.
source: Notably, SK encodes a small conductance Ca2+-activated K+ channel, which can be activated by dendritic Ca2+ influx, and therefore could be one of the major factors underlying hyperpolarization.
evidence: This is a reasoning based on the known properties of SK channels and the experimental results.

claim: SK knockdown increased the firing properties including the US number, peak number and maximum firing rate, even with low laser powers.
source: We then found that SK knockdown increased the firing properties, including the US number, peak number and maximum firing rate, even with low laser powers (Figure 3A–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study testing SK knockdown at different stimulus intensities.

claim: SK knockdown shortened the pause periods (median: ppk-Gal4 103.9 ms, UAS-SK RNAi 112.9 ms, ppk>SK RNAi 46.75 ms).
source: Importantly, the SK knockdown shortened the pause periods (Figure 3E; median of pause period: [ppk-Gal4] 103.9 ms, [UAS-SK RNAi] 112.9 ms, [ppk>SK RNAi] 46.75 ms; p<0.001, Student's t-test with Holm correction)
evidence: This is a key quantitative finding from the current study showing SK's role in pause generation.

claim: SK-dependent current regulates the pause period in Class IV neurons.
source: Importantly, the SK knockdown shortened the pause periods (Figure 3E; median of pause period: [ppk-Gal4] 103.9 ms, [UAS-SK RNAi] 112.9 ms, [ppk>SK RNAi] 46.75 ms; p<0.001, Student's t-test with Holm correction), which suggested that SK-dependent current regulates the pause period.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pause period data.

claim: SK channels are dramatically activated by the sudden increase in intracellular Ca2+ concentration through L-type VGCCs and generate a transient hyperpolarizing K+ current.
source: We speculated that SK channels would be dramatically activated by the sudden increase in [Ca2+]i through L-type VGCCs, and would generate a transient hyperpolarizing K+ current.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis proposed to explain the observed effects of SK knockdown.

claim: The altered physiological responses in SK knockdown neurons were not due to morphological defects in the dendritic arbors.
source: We quantified the dendritic morphology of SK knockdown neurons and concluded that the altered physiological responses were not due to morphological defects in the dendritic arbors (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a control experiment ruling out morphological changes as an explanation for the physiological phenotype.

claim: SK knockdown larvae displayed significantly faster onsets of responses to thermal stimulation at 44°C.
source: To test this hypothesis, we examined how SK knockdown larvae responded to thermal stimulation, and we found that they displayed significantly faster onsets of responses; moreover, the response rate was increased upon moderate stimulation (44°C, Figure 3F and G; 42°C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2E F).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from the current study showing the functional consequence of SK knockdown.

claim: The response rate of SK knockdown larvae was increased upon moderate thermal stimulation (44°C).
source: To test this hypothesis, we examined how SK knockdown larvae responded to thermal stimulation, and we found that they displayed significantly faster onsets of responses; moreover, the response rate was increased upon moderate stimulation (44°C, Figure 3F and G; 42°C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2E F).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from the current study.

claim: The burst-and-pause firing patterns should be output signals provoking robust avoidance behavior.
source: Consistent with these findings, we propose that the burst-and-pause firing patterns should be output signals provoking the robust avoidance behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined electrophysiological and behavioral data.

claim: Knockdown larvae of Shal, Irk2, and Task7 did not show any difference in the response rate of heat avoidance behavior.
source: We also examined heat avoidance behavior of larvae, where one of the other three candidate genes (Shal, Irk2, and Task7) was knocked down; however, the respective knockdown larvae did not show any difference in the response rate of avoidance (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A and B).
evidence: This is a negative result from behavioral testing of other K+ channel knockdowns.

claim: The frequencies of spontaneous spikes were significantly increased in Shal, Irk2, and Task7 knockdown Class IV neurons but not in SK knockdown ones.
source: Interestingly, the frequencies of spontaneous spikes were significantly increased in the three knockdown Class IV neurons but not in SK knockdown ones (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C and D).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study distinguishing SK from other K+ channels.

claim: Elevated basal neuronal activity during development might decrease the efficacy of synaptic transmission and/or remodel synaptic connections of Class IV neurons.
source: Thus, the elevated basal neuronal activity during development might decrease the efficacy of synaptic transmission and/or remodel synaptic connections of the neurons, which would tend to counteract the effect of the increment of firing rate fluctuations on the avoidance behavior of these knockdown animals.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain why Shal, Irk2, and Task7 knockdowns don't show behavioral changes despite increased firing fluctuations.

claim: The numbers of burst-and-pause patterns were significantly different between continuous and intermittent optogenetic illuminations of Class IV neurons.
source: We first investigated firing patterns induced by optogenetic activations in Class IV neurons and found that the numbers of burst-and-pause patterns were significantly different between continuous and intermittent illuminations (Figure 3—figure supplement 5B–D; p<0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank sum test).
evidence: This is a finding from optogenetic experiments in the current study.

claim: The total spike numbers and maximum firing rates were comparable between continuous and intermittent optogenetic illumination conditions.
source: Importantly, the total spike numbers and maximum firing rates were comparable between the two conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 5E and F).
evidence: This is a control finding showing that the two optogenetic conditions differ in fluctuation patterns but not overall firing rate.

claim: The maximum amplitude of Ca2+ rises in Goro neurons was larger upon activation accompanied with more burst-and-pause firing patterns in Class IV neurons.
source: We found that the maximum amplitude of Ca2+ rises in Goro neurons was larger upon activation accompanied with more burst-and-pause firing patterns in Class IV neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 5G and H; [continuous] Fpeak = 11.3 ± 1.8%, [intermittent] Fpeak = 19.4 ± 2.2%, mean ± s.e.m.; p<0.01, Welch's t-test).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study showing that downstream neurons respond differently to different firing patterns.

claim: Firing rate fluctuations are decoded in downstream circuits separately from the firing rate itself.
source: The results suggested that firing rate fluctuations were decoded in downstream circuits separately from the firing rate itself.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the optogenetic and downstream Ca2+ imaging experiments.

claim: Before USs occur, most SK channels are in the steady state because Ca2+/calmodulin association is restricted at low intracellular Ca2+ concentration, and the SK current slightly inhibits the incidence of firings during burst periods.
source: Before USs occur, most SK channels are in the steady state because the Ca2+/calmodulin association is restricted at low [Ca2+]i, and the SK current slightly inhibits the incidence of firings during burst periods.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation proposed in the Discussion to explain the dual role of SK channels.

claim: After USs occur with dendritic Ca2+ transients, SK channels are shifted to the activation state by high intracellular Ca2+ concentration, and the current greatly promotes after-hyperpolarization which generates the pause periods.
source: In contrast, after USs occur with dendritic Ca2+ transients, the channels are shifted to the activation state by high [Ca2+]i, and the current greatly promotes after-hyperpolarization, which generates the pause periods.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation for how SK channels generate pause periods.

claim: SK knockdown attenuates the inhibition of firings, which raises the occurrence rate of USs.
source: Therefore, SK knockdown attenuates the inhibition of firings, which raises the occurrence rate of USs.
evidence: This is an explanation for one effect of SK knockdown based on the proposed mechanism.

claim: SK knockdown dramatically decreases the pause periods, which shortens the time requiring one burst-and-pause firing pattern.
source: In contrast, after USs occur with dendritic Ca2+ transients, the channels are shifted to the activation state by high [Ca2+]i, and the current greatly promotes after-hyperpolarization, which generates the pause periods. Thus, the knockdown dramatically decreases the pause periods, which shortens the time requiring one burst-and-pause firing pattern.
evidence: This is an explanation for another effect of SK knockdown.

claim: The US number per unit time would be expected to increase upon SK knockdown due to two impacts on firings.
source: Due to the two impacts on firings, the US number per unit time would be expected to increase upon SK knockdown.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the proposed dual mechanism of SK channel action.

claim: Once the membrane potential of soma exceeds a certain threshold by prolonged stimulation, Class IV neurons evoke action potentials and then increase firing rates with the intensity of stimulation.
source: (2) Once the membrane potential of soma exceeds a certain threshold by the prolonged stimulation, the neurons evoke action potentials and then increase firing rates with the intensity of stimulation ('rate coding').
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanistic model describing rate coding.

claim: When L-type VGCCs in the dendritic arbors are activated by high-order depolarization, they induce a large Ca2+ influx which rapidly activates SK channels.
source: (3) When L-type VGCCs in the dendritic arbors are activated by the high-order depolarization, they induce a large Ca2+ influx, which rapidly activates SK channels.
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanistic model linking L-type VGCCs to SK channel activation.

claim: Activated SK channels produce a hyperpolarizing current, thereby generating the pause periods.
source: (4) The activated SK channels produce a hyperpolarizing current, thereby generating the pause periods ('fluctuation coding').
evidence: This is the key mechanistic conclusion of the study.

claim: Other K+ channels may slightly contribute to the generation of pauses because the pause periods were not completely abolished in SK knockdown neurons.
source: We also suggest that other K+ channels may slightly contribute to the generation of pauses, because the pause periods were not completely abolished in SK knockdown neurons (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the incomplete abolition of pauses in SK knockdown.

claim: Most voltage-dependent K+ channels hyperpolarize the membrane potential to some degree after depolarization, regardless of dendritic Ca2+ influx.
source: Although the other candidate channels, such as Sh and Shal, are not activated by the [Ca2+]i rise, most of them are voltage-dependent and hence hyperpolarize the membrane potential to some degree after depolarization, regardless of dendritic Ca2+ influx.
evidence: This is an explanation based on known properties of voltage-gated K+ channels.

claim: The hyperpolarization from voltage-dependent K+ channels suppresses the probability of firing, including US, so knockdown of those channels should lead to the increment of the US number.
source: Because the hyperpolarization suppresses the probability of firing, including US, the knockdown of those channels should lead to the increment of the US number.
evidence: This is a logical inference explaining why other K+ channel knockdowns increase US number.

claim: In mammalian cerebellar cortex, climbing fiber inputs evoke complex spikes of Purkinje cells which induce a dendritic Ca2+ influx through Ca2+ spikes and subsequent pauses.
source: In the mammalian cerebellar cortex, climbing fiber inputs evoke complex spikes of Purkinje cells, which induce a dendritic Ca2+ influx through Ca2+ spikes and subsequent pauses (Davie et al., 2008; Kitamura and Häusser, 2011; Llinás and Sugimori, 1980; Mathews et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a summary of established knowledge about Purkinje cells, supported by citations.

claim: The pause periods of post-complex spikes in Purkinje cells are regulated by dendritic Ca2+ spikes which are dependent on P/Q-type VGCCs.
source: The pause periods of post-complex spikes are regulated by dendritic Ca2+ spikes, which are dependent on P/Q-type VGCCs (Davie et al., 2008), and are modulated by after-hyperpolarization, which is largely dependent on SK2 channels (Grasselli et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Purkinje cell physiology, supported by citations.

claim: The pause periods of post-complex spikes in Purkinje cells are modulated by after-hyperpolarization which is largely dependent on SK2 channels.
source: The pause periods of post-complex spikes are regulated by dendritic Ca2+ spikes, which are dependent on P/Q-type VGCCs (Davie et al., 2008), and are modulated by after-hyperpolarization, which is largely dependent on SK2 channels (Grasselli et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Purkinje cell physiology, supported by citation.

claim: The regulatory mechanism of complex spikes in Purkinje cells is remarkably similar to that of burst-and-pause firing patterns in Class IV neurons.
source: Considering these observations, the regulatory mechanism of complex spikes is remarkably similar to that of burst-and-pause firing patterns in Class IV neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a comparative conclusion drawn in the Discussion.

claim: Rate coding occurs in Class IV neurons at relatively low temperatures and is mediated by thermosensitive channels and many types of voltage-gated ion channels.
source: This form of rate coding also occurs in Class IV neurons at relatively low temperatures, and it is mediated by thermosensitive channels and many types of voltage-gated ion channels (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is a summary statement about rate coding in Class IV neurons.

claim: At higher temperature, L-type VGCCs and SK channels modulate the firing, transitioning from continuous high-frequency patterns into burst-and-pause patterns.
source: At higher temperature, however, L-type VGCCs and SK channels modulate the firing, transitioning from continuous high-frequency patterns into burst-and-pause patterns.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: Firing-rate-fluctuation coding allows sensory neurons to transmit strong stimuli not covered in rate coding, thereby provoking robust avoidance behavior.
source: Thus, we propose that the firing-rate-fluctuation coding allows sensory neurons to transmit strong stimuli not covered in rate coding, thereby provoking robust avoidance behavior.
evidence: This is the main conclusion and proposed model of the study.

claim: Trials without USs did not generate Ca2+ transients (n = 19 cells; ΔF/F0 = 0.52 ± 0.87%, mean ± s.e.m. after laser irradiation).
source: (B) Trials without USs did not generate Ca2+ transients (n = 19 cells; ΔF/F0 = 0.52 ± 0.87%, mean ± s.e.m. after laser irradiation).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from Figure 1B showing the relationship between USs and Ca2+ transients.

claim: Trials with USs generated Ca2+ transients (n = 25 cells; ΔF/F0 = 9.33 ± 1.57%, mean ± s.e.m. after laser irradiation).
source: (C) Trials with USs generated Ca2+ transients (n = 25 cells; ΔF/F0 = 9.33 ± 1.57%, mean ± s.e.m. after laser irradiation).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from Figure 1C showing Ca2+ transient amplitudes in US trials.

claim: The first USs occurred at 0.55 ± 0.04 s (mean ± s.e.m.) after the start of laser irradiation.
source: The first USs occurred at 0.55 ± 0.04 s (mean ± s.e.m.).
evidence: This is a timing measurement from Figure 1C.

claim: The maximum firing rates of US trials was larger than that of non-US ones.
source: The maximum firing rates of US trials (Figure 1C) was larger than that of non-US ones (Figure 1B; mean ± s.e.m.; ***p<0.001, Student's t-test with Bonferroni correction)
evidence: This is a statistical comparison from Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The maximum firing rate did not significantly change among trials with varying numbers of US.
source: but it did not significantly change among trials with varying numbers of US.
evidence: This is a finding from Figure 1—figure supplement 1B showing that US number doesn't correlate with maximum firing rate.

claim: Amplitudes of ΔRpeak of SuperClomeleon increased with IR-laser power.
source: (C) Amplitudes of ΔRpeak of SuperClomeleon increased with IR-laser power (mean ± s.e.m.; ***p<0.001, Student's t-test).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from Figure 2C showing dose-dependent Cl− changes.

claim: The US number increased in five different gene knockdown neurons (Sh, Shal, SK, Irk2 and Task7).
source: (E) Boxplot of the total US number in screened neurons. The US number increased in five different gene knockdown neurons (Sh, Shal, SK, Irk2 and Task7; Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: This is a summary of the screening results from Figure 2E.

claim: The amplitudes of dendritic Ca2+ transients did not decrease in the five K+ channel knockdowns except for Ca-α1D RNAi neurons.
source: (F) Amplitudes of the dendritic Ca2+ transients in screened channels. The amplitudes did not decrease except for Ca-α1D RNAi neurons (mean ± s.e.m.; Student's t-test).
evidence: This is a result from Figure 2F showing that K+ channel knockdowns don't affect Ca2+ transients.

claim: SK knockdown neurons increased the US number, peak number with three different laser powers (36, 40, and 48 mW).
source: (B–D) SK knockdown neurons increased the US number, peak number (B and C; boxplots; Wilcoxon rank sum test with Holm correction), and amplitude of the dendritic Ca2+ transients (D; mean ± s.e.m.; Student's t-test with Holm correction) with three different laser powers.
evidence: This is a summary of results from Figure 3B-D showing dose-dependent effects of SK knockdown.

claim: SK knockdown neurons increased the amplitude of the dendritic Ca2+ transients with three different laser powers.
source: (B–D) SK knockdown neurons increased the US number, peak number (B and C; boxplots; Wilcoxon rank sum test with Holm correction), and amplitude of the dendritic Ca2+ transients (D; mean ± s.e.m.; Student's t-test with Holm correction) with three different laser powers.
evidence: This is a result from Figure 3D showing that SK knockdown affects Ca2+ transient amplitude.
